newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian police put down eighth garment protest. [CORRECTED 8:42 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Cambodian police put down eighth garment protest. [CORRECTED 8:42 GMT]

text.p: About 100 police broke up Cambodia's eighth garment worker protest in recent weeks on Wednesday, forcing opposition leader Sam Rainsy off factory property.
Analysts said the government appeared fed up with Rainsy's role in recent worker unrest, which has triggered fears that foreign investors could be scared away.
"This has become a political issue. This is no longer about worker discontent," said Van Sou Ieng, who heads Cambodia's association of garment manufacturers.

He said manufacturers had already implemented industry-wide concessions to workers last week, including higher pay, maternity and sick leave and new overtime policies, and that Wednesday's dispute was politically motivated.
"The situation is now out of (the manufacturers') hands. It has to be dealt with by the government authorities," he said.

The demonstration was the third at Hong Kong-owned Tack Fat Garments and the eighth garment protest since Rainsy, leader of the unrecognised Khmer Nation Party, formed a trade union for workers in Cambodia's burgeoning garment sector last month.
Rainsy, who has led each of the recent demonstrations, stood outside the factory on Wednesday to urge the hundreds of young women reporting for work to join his protest.

Chief of Penal Police Mok Chito later wrenched away the politician's megaphone and pushed him and his bodyguards across the street. Sam Rainsy then got into a car and drove away, and the remaining workers went into the factory under police escort.

Two representatives of Tack Fat, who had flown in from Hong Kong to resolve the dispute, said they were frustrated with the situation, noting they had already come to an agreement with 12 worker representatives on Saturday.
On the factory floor, workers collected their monthly pay but did not return to work.
One representative said the company was rethinking its investment in Cambodia.
"Next time, we'll go to Mexico," he said.
Van Sou Ieng said the worker unrest was caused by "outside agitators", and was leading to delays in new factory construction and canceled orders from wary retailers.
The garment sector is Cambodia's fatest-growing industry, with 36 factories employing over 16,000 workers.
